I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm that it is of an acceptable scientific standard, however I have significant reservations, as outlined above.

In the submitted manuscript, the authors studied the effects of artificially induced high altitude on acute performance changes during aerobic (AE) and anaerobic (ANE) threshold exercises in elite young cross-country skiers with a use of a double-poling cross-country skiing simulator. Results indicated that average HR values at an artificially induced high altitude were higher compared to the lower altitude, but no differences were observed for lactate concentration.

The topic is of interest but there are issues that need to be addressed, as mentioned in the following comments.

Comments 
                Abstract = Background: it is recommended to use “Among the key factors…”; Results for HR: please, clarify “both statistically (p<0.05) and substantively” (mainly the latter).
                    Background = Further elaboration is recommended regarding the examined parameters (HR, La, body fat) in the context of work physiology and their impact in cross-country skiing performance. In addition, further information is required for the introduction of the aerobic and anaerobic threshold levels. This will also help to strengthen the rationale of the study. Finally, provide details why body fat will be assessed in this study and its effect on both actual cross-country skiing performance and measures.
                    Methodology = Provide the rationale to set the valve at level 7 for all participants rather than to provide an individualized resistance. In addition, further information is required for the skinfold measures (caliper details, equation/method used to estimate body fat). Also, provide further information about how the AE and ANE were set. Finally, note these specific comments: “the greater the force applied, the greater the resistance created by the ergometer” and “The measurements were summed”.
                    Statistical analysis = Provide evidence to establish the use of parametric tests, namely which one of the two tests was used. In addition, include information if a statistical software was used.
                    Results = Please, clarify “substantively”. Also, depict the results for bodyfat.

Summary

Cross-sectional survey of patients attending five randomly selected Ayurvedic centres in Udupi Taluk (June–Dec 2022) using the PHQ-9 and Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) to estimate prevalence and investigate associations between stress/depression and sociodemographic factors. Sample size reported as 423 (calculated from 384 + 10% nonresponse). Major Strengths 
                Topical and understudied setting: Studying mental health in patients attending Ayurvedic centres addresses a real gap in integrative/alternative care contexts.
                    Use of validated instruments & open data: The PHQ-9 and PSS are established tools; the anonymised dataset and questionnaire are shared on Figshare (good reproducibility practice).
                    Ethics documented: Institutional Ethics Committee approval and written informed consent are clearly stated (IEC No: 866-2021). Major Concerns 
                Inconsistency in reported sample size / participant count: Methods mention 423 participants but Results state 430; needs clarification and explanation of exclusions or errors.
                    Extremely skewed stress distribution: 93% moderate stress is highly unusual — authors should specify version, scoring, and categorization of PSS and include descriptive stats for raw scores.
                    Statistical methods insufficiently described: Tests used are unclear; report exact methods, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and consider multivariable analysis.
                    Sampling & representativeness: Discuss potential cluster sampling bias; justify 5-centre selection, show prevalence by centre, and clarify representativeness.
                    Confounding and interpretation: Avoid causal language, discuss unmeasured confounders, and address possible selection bias.
                    Multiple testing & selective reporting: Address risk of type I error; pre-specify hypotheses or adjust for multiple comparisons. Minor Concerns / Presentation Issues 
                Ensure consistency in tables (totals, percentages) and fix all formatting issues.
                    Provide statistical software details, test names, and missing-data handling methods.
                    Add comparison with similar Indian or international studies for context.
                    Add figures (histogram or boxplots for PSS and PHQ-9 scores).
                    Improve typographical consistency (spacing, percentage notation, etc.). Concrete, Actionable Suggestions 
                Resolve N discrepancy and provide participant flow diagram.
                    Report raw instrument data with mean, SD, median, IQR; specify cutoffs and references.
                    Clearly state statistical tests, software, alpha level, and multiple comparison handling.
                    Discuss or account for clustering (centre-level analysis).
                    Revise discussion for causal tone and add limitation details.
                    Improve tables with N, test statistics, and clear p-value alignment.
                    Add data visualization plots for key scales. Recommendation

I confirm that I have read this submission and believe that I have an appropriate level of expertise to state that I do not consider it to be of an acceptable scientific standard, for reasons outlined above.

The article summarizes the common mental health disorders among patients accessing care at selected Ayurvedic hospitals during Covid-19 pandemic. I appreciate the effort of authors in their interest on assessing mental health disorders among patients seeking care at the health facility. Although the topic was interesting I found major concerns associated with the article. Here is a consolidated comments attached below.

Introduction and Rationale:The introduction lacks a logical flow, with disconnected paragraphs that do not build a cohesive argument. It fails to provide sufficient background evidence on the prevalence of common mental health disorders (CMDs) and their contributing factors in the study population, which is essential for establishing context. Furthermore, the study location is inappropriately placed in the introduction rather than the methodology section.

Methodological Weaknesses:The methodology section is notably brief and lacks critical details. It does not adequately describe the activities undertaken during the study, nor does it specify the standard tools or instruments used to assess mental health disorders, exposures, and outcomes. A crucial omission is the absence of a clear explanation of the sample size and the justification for its selection.

Data Analysis and Presentation of Results:The results section is overly descriptive and could be simplified by focusing on the most significant findings rather than detailing every variable. The authors have not appropriately categorized the stress/depression b Additionally, data presented in Table 4 appears to be entirely new information, as it was not mentioned or justified within the methodology section.

Inferences and Confounding Factors: The most critical concern is the absence of logic when attributing the findings to COVID-19. The study's cross-sectional design only captures the patients' mental health at a single point in time. The method section does not distinguish them are Covid-19 patients or other patients. It fails to account for other potential confounding factors, such as the patients' pre-existing health conditions and its relationship with the stress of their current illness, all of which could independently contribute to their mental state. Therefore, the statement that the observed stress and depression levels were a direct result of COVID-19 is an unfounded inference that is not supported by the study's design.

We confirm that we have read this submission and believe that we have an appropriate level of expertise to confirm

The article, “Group Structure and Derivation on PMS-algebras,” presents a compelling investigation. Using mathematical techniques, the researchers analyzed the properties and behavior of derivations within PMS-algebras. Specifically, they demonstrated that the set of all derivations associated with the defined binary operations forms a semi-group. This analysis offers a comprehensive understanding of generalized derivations, d-invariant ideals, fixed sets, and torsion-free PMS-algebras within this algebraic framework.

Overall, the article effectively explores various aspects of torsion-free and generalized PMS-algebras, as well as the group structure and derivations on PMS-algebras. Consequently, this manuscript makes a significant contribution to the study of derivations on PMS-algebras. While the article is rich in proven results, the introduction could be strengthened by explicitly stating the motivation for this research. However, the authors adequately highlighted the study's importance and main contributions in the conclusion part of the manuscript. Therefore, I approved the acceptance for indexing in the journal.

Krupa Shah and coworkers present a systematic review on feto-maternal outcome and delivery in pregnancies of patients with osteogenesis imperfecta. They reviewed 28 articles that were published between January 1975 and January 2025 and reported on pregnancy characteristics, maternal, antenatal, intrapartum and post-partum observations.

This is an important study because due to the scarcity of the disorder there is only limited information available on pregnancies-related complications. The objectives, search strategies, inclusion and exclusion criteria are presented in a detailed manner. In particular, the summary presented in Table 3 is very clear and address properly all points discussed in the study. The authors concluded that there is a crucial need for further research about maternal and neonatal complications associated with OI pregnancies and in fact there are further cohort studies on pregnancy-related complications in patients with osteogenesis imperfecta published since the end of the recorded period of the present review.

                Tables and figures clearly summarize frequencies and distributions.

                Weak Points / Limitations

Tables and figures clearly summarize frequencies and distributions.

The Results section is logically structured and easy to follow.

1. Major Conceptual Limitation: “Prevalence” Is Misused 
                The study reports 100 incidents but does not define a denominator (total number of students/staff or person-years).
                    Therefore, true prevalence or incidence rates cannot be calculated.
                    The manuscript should be framed as a descriptive analysis of reported exposure incidents, not a prevalence study. 
                2. Outcome Variable Is Poorly Defined 
                The manuscript states that the “dependent variable” is occurrence of exposure injuries, yet all included records already represent exposure injuries.
                    This creates a logical inconsistency: there is no non-exposed comparison group.
                    Consequently, several chi-square analyses are methodologically inappropriate. 
                3. Statistical Analysis Is Limited and Sometimes Misapplied 
                Exclusive reliance on bivariate chi-square tests limits interpretability.
                    No multivariable analysis was performed to control for confounding (e.g., gender vs. role vs. session timing).
                    Small cell sizes (including zero counts) violate assumptions of chi-square testing in some tables. 
                4. Interpretation Overreaches the Data 
                Statements such as “incidence was high” are not supported without institutional or national benchmarks.
                    Gender differences are discussed as potential biological or psychological phenomena, yet reporting behavior bias is not adequately addressed.
                    The manuscript occasionally implies causal relationships, which is inappropriate for a retrospective descriptive study. 
                5. Limited Generalizability 
                Data were collected from a single academic institution.
                    Institutional protocols, reporting culture, and supervision intensity may differ substantially from other settings.
                    Findings should be interpreted as context-specific, but this is not emphasized enough. 
                6. Incomplete Exploration of Underreporting 
                While underreporting is acknowledged in the Introduction and Discussion, the study design cannot assess the magnitude of underreporting.
                    This weakens conclusions related to frequency and risk patterns. 
                7. Discussion Is Overly Long and Repetitive 
                The Discussion section heavily reiterates previously published findings without sufficiently distinguishing what is novel in this study.
                    Some cited literature is used descriptively rather than analytically.

This article presents a hybrid deep learning framework (BiLSTM+CNN with stacked Random Forest) for predicting breast cancer survival using multi-omics data from the METABRIC and TCGA datasets. The authors integrate clinical, copy number alteration, and gene expression features with MRMR feature selection and evaluate performance using cross-validation and ROC-based metrics. The study reports high predictive accuracy and demonstrates external validation across datasets, suggesting robustness and potential clinical relevance.

The manuscript is clearly structured and generally well written. The background appropriately situates the work within recent literature on multi-omics survival modeling. However, claims regarding interpretability and clinical applicability would benefit from more explicit demonstrations (e.g., feature importance analysis linked to biological pathways). This is a 
                recommended improvement, not a requirement for scientific soundness.

The use of two independent public datasets, cross-validation, and standard evaluation metrics constitutes an appropriate and technically sound design. External validation strengthens the conclusions. An ablation study isolating the contribution of each architectural component would further support claims of model superiority but is optional.

While the authors provide architecture details and public code, several aspects limit full replication. To ensure scientific soundness, the authors 
                must: (1) specify exact preprocessing pipelines and parameter settings for MRMR and data augmentation; (2) document all random seeds and data splits; and (3) describe the computational environment (hardware/software versions). Providing a step-by-step reproducibility protocol or configuration file would resolve these issues.

The evaluation metrics and cross-validation strategy are appropriate. Including formal statistical comparisons between models or calibration analyses would strengthen rigor but is not essential.

Public datasets and open code support reproducibility. The conclusions are broadly supported by the results, though statements about clinical impact should be moderated or accompanied by discussion of deployment limitations.

Overall, the article is scientifically promising. Addressing the required reproducibility clarifications will make it methodologically robust.
